Whole blue mallow blossoms, hand-picked daily and dried with their color intact. Deeply mucilaginous, and it turns your tea indigo.

Blue mallow (*Malva sylvestris*) has to be picked blossom by blossom, every morning through the bloom, and dried immediately or the petals brown. It is the most labor-intensive thing we dry, and worth every minute of it.

Poured over with hot water the flowers release a soft, slippery mucilage traditionally used to soothe dry throats and irritated tissue — and they throw an astonishing indigo blue that shifts to violet and pink when you add lemon.

Sold by the half ounce because these blossoms are almost weightless. A half ounce is a lot of flowers.

## How to Prepare

Steep 1 tablespoon of whole flowers per 8 oz of water, covered, for 10 minutes. For maximum mucilage, cold-infuse overnight in the refrigerator instead — heat is hard on demulcents.

## Ingredients

Whole resinous calendula heads, not just the petals. Sticky, golden, and the foundation of nearly every salve we make.

We pick calendula (*Calendula officinalis*) every other day from June until frost — the more you pick, the more it blooms. These are whole flower heads, green base and all, because the resin concentrates right there where the petals meet the calyx. Petal-only calendula looks prettier and does considerably less.

If your fingers come away sticky from handling it, that is the resin, and that is what you are paying for. This is the herb we infuse into oil for our salve, and the one we recommend most often to people making their own.

## How to Prepare

**Infused oil:** Fill a jar loosely with flowers, cover completely with olive or jojoba oil, and let it sit 4-6 weeks out of direct sun. Strain well. Use as-is or thicken with beeswax for a salve.

**Tea or skin wash:** Steep 1 tablespoon per 8 oz of hot water, covered, for 15 minutes. Cool before applying externally.

Farm-grown skullcap aerial parts, harvested in flower and shade-dried. A classic nervine for frazzled nerves and restless evenings.

Skullcap (*Scutellaria lateriflora*) is one of the herbs we are most protective of at harvest. We cut the aerial parts just as the small hooded flowers open along the stem, then shade-dry them slowly on screens so the color and aroma stay intact. Rushed or sun-dried skullcap loses most of what makes it worth growing.

Traditionally used as a nervine for a mind that will not stop circling — tense shoulders, racing thoughts at bedtime, the wired-and-tired feeling at the end of a long week.

## How to Prepare

Steep 1 teaspoon per 8 oz of just-boiled water, covered, for 10-15 minutes. Drink in the evening. Pairs beautifully with lemon balm.

Yarrow flower and leaf harvested at peak bloom. Aromatic, bitter, and pungent — the herbalist's field-and-medicine-chest staple.

Yarrow (*Achillea millefolium*) has been in the herbalist's kit for as long as there have been herbalists. We harvest the flowering tops with a portion of the feathery leaf at full bloom, when the aroma is sharpest, and dry them whole before cutting.

Traditionally used as a diaphoretic tea at the first chill of a cold, and externally as a wash or compress. Distinctly bitter and aromatic — this is not a beverage tea, and it is not meant to be.

## How to Prepare

**Tea:** Steep 1 teaspoon per 8 oz of hot water, covered, for 10 minutes. Best taken hot.

**External wash:** Steep 1 tablespoon per cup, cool completely, and apply with a clean cloth.

Avoid during pregnancy. Yarrow is in the aster family — skip it if you react to that family.
